platforms.title: 3 At-Home Tests That Can Reveal Early Sarcopenia
platforms.meta_description: Sarcopenia has no pain, so most people miss it. EWGSOP2 grip strength and chair stand cutoffs let you screen yourself at home with a chair and a jar lid.
platforms.body_html:
Sarcopenia doesn't hurt, which is exactly why most people don't catch it until stairs feel unreasonably hard. But there are three simple checks you can do at home with nothing more than a tape measure and a chair. The European Working Group on Sarcopenia in Older People (EWGSOP2), in its 2019 consensus published in Age and Ageing, lays out grip strength and the chair stand test as the two standard ways to screen for low muscle strength, alongside the SARC-F questionnaire.

Why Grip Strength Is the First Thing to Check

EWGSOP2 defines low grip strength as under 27 kg for men and under 16 kg for women — measured with a hand dynamometer, though a rough real-world proxy is how hard it is to twist open a stubborn jar lid or wring out a wet towel. Grip strength correlates strongly with overall muscle strength, which is why it's used as a quick, equipment-light stand-in rather than testing every muscle group individually.

The second test, the chair stand test, measures leg strength: rise from a seated chair five times in a row without using your arms, and time it. EWGSOP2 flags a result over 15 seconds (or being unable to complete it at all) as low muscle strength. Because this test requires both strength and endurance in the legs, it's a convenient stand-in for quadriceps strength testing that would otherwise require a lab.

So What Do You Actually Do With the Results?

Time yourself doing five chair stands without arm support. Test your grip against a jar lid or, if you have one, an actual hand dynamometer. Neither test on its own is a diagnosis — EWGSOP2 recommends these as a first-pass screen, with a formal diagnosis confirmed afterward by muscle mass measurement (DXA or bioelectrical impedance analysis) at a clinic. If either result falls outside the cutoffs, or your chair-stand time is right on the border, that's the signal to bring it up with a doctor rather than write it off as "just getting older."

It's worth being honest about the limits here: these are screening tools, not diagnostic ones. The SARC-F questionnaire in particular has low-to-moderate sensitivity and very high specificity, meaning it mostly catches more severe cases and can miss milder, earlier sarcopenia — a normal result doesn't fully rule it out, especially if something still feels off.

None of this replaces the deeper causes worth addressing either — resistance training and adequate protein intake are still what actually rebuilds muscle over time. What these two tests add is an earlier warning: catching a borderline result now, while it's still easy to reverse with exercise and diet, beats noticing it only once climbing a single flight of stairs has become genuinely difficult.

Quick checklist: grip strength under 27 kg (men) or 16 kg (women); five chair stands taking longer than 15 seconds; either test near the cutoff rather than clearly normal. If any of these apply, don't self-diagnose from here — ask your doctor about a proper muscle mass assessment.
